overview.intro: Comprehension pays the candidate for reading carefully and answering exactly what was asked. The passage is unseen, so no preparation can substitute for the minutes you give it: read once for the shape of the argument, then return to each question and locate its paragraph before writing. This chapter works the four question families the paper uses — retrieval, vocabulary in context, inference and reference — each with its own technique: retrieval rewards quoting the passage’s own words; vocabulary questions ask what the word means here, not everywhere; inference requires evidence plus a stated conclusion; reference questions demand the antecedent, not a guess. The chapter then trains the summary task, where strict word limits and content units decide the mark, and closes with the answer-writing habits that keep near-misses from becoming lost marks.

learningOutcomes: Locate the answering paragraph for a question before attempting an answer.
Define vocabulary as it functions in its passage context rather than in isolation.
Draw inferences that cite textual evidence for the conclusion drawn.
Identify the antecedent of reference words such as it, they, this and which.
Write a summary within a stated word limit that covers the passage’s content units.

learn.title: Two passes and the art of locating the answer

blocks.text: The unseen passage is not read for pleasure in an examination; it is read for structure first and detail second. The first pass takes three minutes and asks only what the passage is doing — arguing, narrating, explaining or evaluating — and where each paragraph’s contribution sits; notes of five words per paragraph are enough to build a map. The second pass is question by question: read the question, underline its controlling word, find the paragraph that answers it, and only then write. This order prevents the commonest failure, which is answering from memory of the wrong paragraph in fluent language that the passage does not support. Retrieval questions want the passage’s own words quoted rather than paraphrased, because the examiner matches against the text. Every answer should be complete as a sentence even when the question is a fragment, and the mark is for what is written, not what was understood privately.

items: First pass: name the passage’s job and give each paragraph a five-word label.
Second pass: question by question, locating the answering paragraph before writing.
Underline the controlling word in the question: why, how far, what evidence, which word.
Retrieval answers quote the passage; paraphrase invites accidental drift.
Write every answer as a complete sentence, even when the question is a fragment.

items.note: Underline made … hesitate, find the paragraph containing the pause, quote the stated cause rather than a plausible one.

items.text: Tempting drift: the passage says the road was “barely passable”, answer writes “dangerous”.
items.note: The examiner looks for barely passable; the near-synonym costs the retrieval mark.

learn.title: Vocabulary in context and reference tracking

blocks.text: A vocabulary question is a question about this passage, not about the language in general, and the method that fails is recalling the word’s commonest sense. Instead, substitute each candidate meaning back into the sentence: the right one keeps the grammar, the tone and the argument intact, while a wrong one breaks at least one of the three. Tone matters as much as sense — a word used dismissively cannot mean what its neutral dictionary entry offers. Reference tracking works backwards: for it, they, this, that or which, read the sentence before and ask what noun could grammatically and logically perform the role the pronoun plays; if two candidates appear, test which one survives the pronoun’s action or quality. Ambiguous references are usually resolved by proximity and by number, singular pronouns preferring singular antecedents nearby. When a reference word points at a whole clause rather than a noun, name the clause’s content in your answer instead of hunting for a noun that does not exist.

items: Substitute candidate meanings into the sentence; the right one keeps grammar, tone and sense.
Tone is part of meaning: dismissive, approving and neutral uses of one word differ.
Trace reference words backwards to the nearest grammatically possible antecedent.
Check number: singular pronouns prefer singular nouns, plural prefer plural.
A pronoun may refer to a whole clause — answer with the clause’s content, not a noun.
Quote the surrounding phrase as evidence when explaining a reference choice.

items.text: “His protest was loudest where it mattered least.” — What does it refer to?
items.note: The clause where it mattered least points to the forum of the decision; it stands for the occasion, not a noun in the previous sentence.

items.text: “The old method proved serviceable.” — serviceable here means
items.note: Fit for purpose in this context; substituting “outdated” breaks the approval the sentence records.

items.meaning: The noun or clause a pronoun refers back to.
A word’s sense as fixed by this passage rather than by general usage.
The attitude a word or passage reveals towards its subject.
The quoted line that proves the inference an answer draws.

blocks.text: Inference is the question family that separates readers who enjoyed the passage from readers who understood it, and its mark scheme has two halves that must both appear in the answer: the conclusion and the evidence that licenses it. An answer that states only the conclusion looks like a guess; an answer that quotes only the evidence has not committed to a reading. The disciplined form is therefore one sentence of claim and one of proof — “The narrator regrets the decision, because the passage describes the journey as undertaken ‘against every judgement I had’.” Evidence must be quoted or precisely paraphrased from the answering paragraph, never imported from general knowledge, because the examiner checks answers against the text alone. Degree words in questions — how far, to what extent, why — demand calibrated answers: acknowledge the limit of the evidence before asserting the conclusion. Where two readings survive the evidence, the stronger one is the one that explains more of the passage with fewer exceptions.

items: Every inference carries two halves: the conclusion and the quoted evidence.
Evidence comes from the answering paragraph, never from general knowledge.
Degree words ask for calibration: state what the evidence supports and where it stops.
Prefer the reading that explains the most text with the fewest exceptions.
If the passage hedges — seemed, perhaps, partly — hedge in the same degree.
One precise quotation beats three vague paraphrases.

items.note: Strong: “The tone is critical: the policy is called ‘elegant on paper’ before the failure is described, which praises the design while condemning the result.”
The passage opposes this reform; the evidence never generalises to all, so the answer must not.

items.meaning: A conclusion drawn from evidence in the text rather than stated outright.
Matching the strength of the claim to the strength of the evidence.
A deliberate softening word such as seemed or partly, matching textual caution.
The reason the evidence supports the conclusion being drawn.

learn.title: Summary writing inside the word limit

blocks.text: The summary is a content-unit exercise wearing the clothes of a writing task. Before drafting, list the units the passage offers — typically five to eight for a marked summary — and rank them by what the question asks for; units the question excludes are cut even if they are interesting. The draft then compresses each unit into a clause, joins clauses with economical connectives and counts the words. Within the limit, variety of vocabulary and structure is itself marked: a summary written entirely in the passage’s own words shows no command of compression, while one written entirely in synonyms drifts from the source. Units are separated by full stops or semicolons so the examiner can count them, and the two most common failures are spending the limit on the opening unit and adding an opinion sentence at the end. The final count must exclude no word: if the draft is three words over, cut a relative clause rather than a content unit.

items: List and rank content units first; cut units the question excludes.
One clause per unit; separate units so the examiner can count them.
Compress with synonyms and clause-merging, not by deleting content.
Do not open with the passage’s first sentence verbatim — it shows no command.
Never add opinion, inference or a closing flourish; the summary reports only.
Cut relative clauses to save words; never cut a content unit.

items.text: Unit plus clause: “Because the scheme was underfunded from the start, it collapsed within a term.”
items.note: Two units, six words saved against “The scheme had been underfunded. It collapsed after one term.”

items.text: Over-limit repair: cut “which had been promised since March” — a relative clause, not a unit.
items.note: Content survives intact; the word count falls by seven.

Retrieval quotes the passage’s own words; paraphrase drift costs the mark.
Vocabulary means the meaning here: substitute candidates until grammar, tone and sense fit.
Reference words are traced backwards to the grammatically possible antecedent.
Inference answers carry both halves: conclusion and quoted evidence.
Degree words demand calibrated claims that match the evidence’s strength.
Summary marks follow content units inside the word limit.
Cut relative clauses to save words, never a content unit.
Never add opinion to a summary; report only what the passage states.
Write every answer as a complete sentence, whatever shape the question has.
examFocus: Locate the answering paragraph before writing; fluent answers to the wrong paragraph score zero.
Quote rather than paraphrase in retrieval questions.

vocabulary.meaning: The noun or clause a pronoun refers back to.
A word’s sense as this passage uses it, not its general sense.
A conclusion drawn from textual evidence rather than stated outright.
Matching the strength of a claim to the strength of the evidence.
A softening word such as perhaps that mirrors caution in the source.
One indivisible idea a summary must carry to earn its mark.
The question family asking for a fact stated in the passage.
The reasoning that connects quoted evidence to the conclusion drawn.

questions.prompt: In a comprehension answer, an inference must always include:
options: A conclusion and the evidence supporting it
A synonym for the passage’s key word
A summary of the whole passage
questions.answer: A conclusion and the evidence supporting it
questions.explanation: The mark scheme carries two halves: the conclusion drawn and the textual evidence that licenses it.

questions.prompt: “The proposal was timely but thin.” In this sentence, thin most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The but sets a contrast with timely approval, so the criticism must concern substance rather than appearance.

questions.prompt: When a summary draft exceeds the word limit, the correct repair is to:
options: Cut relative clauses and compress clauses while keeping every content unit
Merge two content units into one
Begin with the passage’s opening sentence
questions.answer: Cut relative clauses and compress clauses while keeping every content unit
questions.explanation: Content units carry the marks; grammatical elaboration around them can be cut without losing any unit.

questions.prompt: A question asks “How far does the passage support the view that the scheme failed?” The best answer:
options: Asserts flatly that the scheme failed
States the degree supported and quotes evidence while acknowledging the limit
Describes the scheme’s history without evaluating it
Answers with a personal anecdote about failure
questions.answer: States the degree supported and quotes evidence while acknowledging the limit
questions.explanation: The degree phrase how far demands calibration: what the evidence supports and where it stops.

questions.prompt: The noun or clause that a pronoun refers back to is called its __________ .
questions.explanation: Tracing the pronoun backwards to a grammatically possible antecedent settles reference questions.

questions.prompt: One indivisible idea that a summary must carry to earn its mark is called a content __________ .
questions.explanation: Marks follow units present within the word limit; cutting a unit to fit loses content marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why quoting the passage is preferred to paraphrasing in a retrieval answer, and state one risk of paraphrasing.
questions.answer: The examiner matches an answer against the source text, so the passage’s own words make the match immediate and unarguable, while a paraphrase must be judged for equivalence before it can be credited. The chief risk of paraphrasing is drift: a near-synonym can quietly shift scope or tone — barely passable becomes dangerous, seemed becomes was — and the shifted claim is no longer the passage’s, so the retrieval mark is withheld even though the answer shows understanding. A second, smaller risk is wasting time on word substitution under examination pressure while the intended meaning could have been copied in fewer seconds.
questions.explanation: Quotation lets the examiner match the answer against the text directly, while paraphrase can shift scope or tone unnoticed.

questions.prompt: Describe the method for finding what a pronoun refers to when two candidate nouns stand nearby.
questions.answer: Read the sentence containing the pronoun and the one before it, then list every noun that could grammatically perform the pronoun’s action or receive its description. Test them in order: number first, since a singular pronoun prefers a singular noun and a plural pronoun a plural one; then proximity, since the nearer candidate usually wins when both remain; then logic, asking which candidate makes the sentence’s action or quality meaningful. If the pronoun stands for an entire clause rather than any noun, answer with the content of that clause instead. Finally quote the confirming phrase, so the answer shows the trace rather than only the result.
questions.explanation: Number, proximity and grammar eliminate candidates in order, and the quoted phrase proves the trace worked.

questions.prompt: A summary of a passage about urban tree loss must be written in exactly 40 words. The passage’s content units are: (1) councils remove trees for pavement damage; (2) the removal is cheaper than root barriers; (3) shade loss raises street temperature; (4) mature trees store far more carbon than saplings; (5) replanting programmes count trees, not maturity; (6) residents report lower wellbeing on denuded streets. Write a 40-word summary covering all six units.
questions.answer: Councils remove trees damaging pavements because cutting costs less than root barriers. Losing shade raises street temperatures, and mature trunks store far more carbon than young replacements. Replanting counts saplings rather than growth, while residents grow gloomier on bare streets.
questions.explanation: Forty words: sentence one carries units one and two (pavement damage and cost), sentence two units three and four (shade loss and carbon storage), sentence three units five and six (counting saplings and wellbeing), with every relative clause cut to fit the limit.

questions.prompt: A candidate answers an inference question with: “The writer probably regretted moving house, and the passage was about moving.” Evaluate this answer against the mark scheme and rewrite it to full marks.
questions.answer: The answer takes only one of the two required halves and mishandles the half it takes. It states a conclusion — regret — but supports it with a topic label, the passage was about moving, which is not evidence at all: a topic cannot license a claim about the writer’s attitude. The word probably also calibrates nothing, since it neither quotes nor concedes anything. Against the two-half mark scheme the conclusion earns nothing without quoted support, so the answer scores near zero despite naming the right feeling. The rewrite states the conclusion and proves it: “The writer regrets the move: the passage describes the first winter there as endured ‘against every judgement I had’, which frames the decision as one the writer now wishes undone.” The quotation comes from the answering paragraph, the warrant in the which-clause connects it to the claim, and the hedge of the original disappears because the evidence carries the degree itself.
questions.explanation: The mark scheme pays for conclusion plus quoted warrant; a topic label supplies neither and scores almost nothing.
